Content: There are five federal filing statuses: Single, Married Filing Jointly, Married Filing Separately, Head of Household, and Qualifying Surviving Spouse. The correct status affects the standard deduction, tax brackets, and eligibility for many credits.
KeyPoints: Single|Married Filing Jointly (MFJ)|Married Filing Separately (MFS)|Head of Household (HOH)|Qualifying Surviving Spouse (QSS)

Content: Filing status questions test whether you know all five options. Single, MFJ, MFS, HOH, and QSS are the only five - memorize the list cold.
Think of filing status as five doors, and every taxpayer walks through exactly one. Single and MFJ are the common ones, HOH and QSS have specific requirements, and MFS is the least common door.

Filing status is based on the taxpayer's marital status on the last day of the tax year, December 31. A taxpayer who is unmarried all year files Single, and a taxpayer married as of December 31 is considered married for the whole year.
KeyPoints: Status is set as of December 31|Married on Dec 31 = married all year|Divorced by Dec 31 = unmarried all year

Content: The exam loves the December 31 snapshot rule. It doesn't matter if a couple married on December 30 - they're treated as married for the entire year.
Picture a single photo taken at midnight on December 31. Whatever your marital status is in that photo is your status for the whole year, no matter what it was in January.

Married Filing Jointly combines both spouses' income and deductions on one return. It usually produces the lowest combined tax and is available to any legally married couple, even if only one spouse had income.
KeyPoints: Combines both spouses' income|Usually the most favorable status|Available even with one earner|Both spouses are jointly liable for the return

Content: MFJ questions usually test that it's available even when only one spouse worked, and that both spouses are on the hook for the whole return.
Think of MFJ as merging two rivers into one - all the income and deductions flow together, and both spouses are responsible for what's downstream.

Married Filing Separately lets each spouse report only their own income and deductions, but it disqualifies the couple from several credits and often results in a higher combined tax bill. It's typically chosen for liability protection or specific tax-planning reasons.
KeyPoints: Each spouse reports own income|Disqualifies several credits (EITC, education credits)|Often higher combined tax|Used for liability separation or planning reasons

Content: MFS almost always shows up on the exam as the status that loses credits. If a question mentions EITC or education credits with MFS, the answer is usually 'not allowed.'
MFS is like keeping separate bank accounts in a marriage - it protects you from your spouse's tax problems, but you give up some perks you'd get by combining finances.

Head of Household requires the taxpayer to be unmarried (or considered unmarried) at year-end, pay more than half the cost of keeping up a home, and have a qualifying person live with them for more than half the year.
KeyPoints: Must be unmarried or considered unmarried|Pay more than half the home's upkeep|Qualifying person lives there more than half the year|Better standard deduction and brackets than Single

Content: HOH has three tests you need cold: unmarried status, more than half the home costs, and a qualifying person living there more than half the year. Miss any one and it's not HOH.
Think of HOH as three keys that all have to turn at once: are you unmarried, are you paying most of the bills, and does someone who counts live with you more than half the year?

A married taxpayer can still qualify for Head of Household under the 'considered unmarried' rule if they lived apart from their spouse for the last six months of the year, filed a separate return, and paid more than half the cost of a home that was the main home of a qualifying child.
KeyPoints: Lived apart from spouse last 6 months|Files a separate return|Paid more than half the home's cost|Home is the main home of a qualifying child

Content: Considered unmarried is the exception the exam loves to test. A married person can still file HOH if they lived apart from their spouse the last six months of the year and meet the other tests.

Picture a couple who split up in June but never finalized a divorce. As long as they lived apart for the last six months and the taxpayer covers the home for their kid, the tax code treats them as unmarried for HOH purposes.

Qualifying Surviving Spouse status is available for up to two tax years after a spouse's death, as long as the taxpayer has a dependent child living with them and paid more than half the cost of keeping up the home. It uses the same standard deduction and tax brackets as Married Filing Jointly.
KeyPoints: Available up to 2 years after spouse's death|Requires a dependent child in the home|Must pay more than half of home upkeep|Same brackets/deduction as MFJ

Content: QSS questions test the two-year window and the dependent child requirement. No dependent child living in the home means no QSS, no matter how recently the spouse died.
Think of QSS as a soft landing after losing a spouse - for two years, if you're raising their child, the tax code lets you keep MFJ-level treatment even though you're now filing alone.

When a taxpayer qualifies for more than one filing status, the preparer should generally choose the one that results in the lowest tax, most often Head of Household over Single, or Married Filing Jointly over Married Filing Separately.
KeyPoints: Compare eligible statuses for the best result|HOH usually beats Single when qualified|MFJ usually beats MFS|Eligibility rules must still be met exactly

Content: When a scenario says a taxpayer qualifies for two statuses, the exam wants the one with the lower tax - but only if the taxpayer truly meets every requirement for it.
Think of filing status like picking the best-priced lane at checkout - you always take the cheaper lane, but only if you actually qualify to stand in it.

Whether a taxpayer must file a return depends on their gross income, filing status, age, and dependency status. The IRS publishes minimum income thresholds each year that trigger a filing requirement.
KeyPoints: Based on gross income, filing status, age|Thresholds are published annually|Different thresholds for dependents|Filing isn't required below the threshold, but may still be beneficial

Content: Filing requirement questions hinge on four factors: income, filing status, age, and dependency status. Missing any one of these changes the threshold.
Think of the filing requirement like a bar that moves depending on who you are - single versus married, under 65 versus 65-plus, dependent versus not. Clear the bar and you must file.

Each filing status has its own gross income threshold that triggers a filing requirement, and the threshold is generally close to the standard deduction for that status. Taxpayers 65 or older get a higher threshold.
KeyPoints: Threshold roughly matches the standard deduction|Varies by filing status|Higher threshold at age 65+|Published annually by the IRS

Content: The exam wants you to know the threshold tracks the standard deduction, and that being 65 or older raises it further.
Think of the filing threshold as roughly equal to your standard deduction - the IRS isn't going to make you file a return just to report income that would be wiped out by your own deduction anyway.
A taxpayer with net self-employment earnings of $400 or more must file a return and pay self-employment tax, even if their total income is below the regular filing threshold.
KeyPoints: $400 net self-employment earnings triggers filing|Applies even below the normal income threshold|Self-employment tax is calculated on Schedule SE|Separate rule from the general filing threshold

Content: This is the exception that trips people up: $400 of net self-employment income forces a filing requirement, even when regular income wouldn't.
Think of self-employment income as having its own trip-wire set much lower than everyone else's - just $400 net earnings and you must file, no matter what your total income looks like.

A dependent must file their own return if their earned income, unearned income, or combined gross income exceeds specific limits that are lower than the limits for non-dependents. Both earned and unearned income thresholds apply, and the lower of the two triggers filing.
KeyPoints: Dependents have their own, lower filing thresholds|Earned income and unearned income both have separate limits|Being claimed as a dependent doesn't remove the filing requirement|Applies even if the dependent owes no tax

Content: Dependent filing thresholds are much lower than regular thresholds, and there are separate limits for earned versus unearned income. Watch for both in a scenario.

Think of a dependent's filing requirement as having two separate trip-wires - one for money they earned working, one for money like interest or dividends - and crossing either one means they have to file.

A taxpayer below the filing threshold may still want to file to claim a refund of withheld taxes or to claim a refundable credit like the Earned Income Tax Credit, even though they aren't legally required to file.
KeyPoints: Filing isn't required but can still be worthwhile|Claims back withheld taxes|Needed to claim refundable credits|No penalty for filing when not required

Content: Remember: not being required to file doesn't mean you shouldn't. Withheld taxes and refundable credits only come back if a return is filed.
Think of it like leaving cash on the table - if taxes were withheld or a refundable credit is available, filing is the only way to actually collect what's owed to you.
A nonresident alien with U.S. source income generally files Form 1040-NR rather than the standard Form 1040, and different rules apply to deductions, credits, and filing status.
KeyPoints: Files Form 1040-NR, not Form 1040|Different deduction and credit rules apply|Based on U.S. source income|Residency tests determine resident vs. nonresident alien status

Content: If a scenario mentions a nonresident alien, the form is 1040-NR, not the standard 1040 - and the deduction and credit rules aren't the same.
Think of Form 1040-NR as a completely different rulebook, built specifically for people who earn U.S. income without being U.S. tax residents.
A qualifying child is a dependent who meets specific relationship, age, residency, support, and joint return tests. Meeting all five tests is required, not just some of them.
KeyPoints: Relationship test|Age test|Residency test|Support test|Joint return test

Content: Qualifying child questions always come back to the same five tests. Missing even one test means the person doesn't qualify as a qualifying child.
Think of the five qualifying child tests as five locks on one door - you need every single key to open it, not just most of them.

ConceptTitle: Relationship Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: The relationship test requires the child to be the taxpayer's son, daughter, stepchild, foster child, sibling, stepsibling, or a descendant of any of them, such as a grandchild, niece, or nephew.
KeyPoints: Son, daughter, stepchild, or foster child|Sibling or stepsibling|Descendants of these relationships qualify too|Unrelated children don't meet this test

ConceptTitle: Relationship Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: The relationship test is about the family tree - direct descendants, siblings, and their descendants all count. An unrelated child never passes this test.

ConceptTitle: Relationship Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: Picture drawing a family tree - kids, grandkids, siblings, nieces and nephews are all on it. If the child isn't somewhere on that tree, the relationship test fails.

ConceptTitle: Age Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: The age test requires the child to be under 19 at year-end, under 24 if a full-time student, or any age if permanently and totally disabled. The child must also be younger than the taxpayer claiming them (except when disabled).
KeyPoints: Under 19, or under 24 if a full-time student|Any age if permanently and totally disabled|Must be younger than the taxpayer (except if disabled)|Full-time student has its own definition

ConceptTitle: Age Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: The age test has three thresholds: 19, 24 for students, and no limit for disability. The exam often tests the student exception specifically.

ConceptTitle: Age Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: Think of the age test like three different finish lines - a regular kid stops qualifying at 19, a full-time student gets to run until 24, and a disabled dependent never hits a finish line at all.

ConceptTitle: Residency Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: The residency test requires the child to have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year. Temporary absences for school, medical care, vacation, or military service still count as time lived at home.
KeyPoints: Must live with taxpayer more than half the year|Temporary absences still count as time at home|School, medical care, and military service are common exceptions|A child born or who died during the year can still meet this test

ConceptTitle: Residency Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: The exam tests the temporary absence exception constantly - a kid away at college is still treated as living at home for this test.

ConceptTitle: Residency Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: Think of temporary absences like a pause button, not a stop button. The clock of 'living at home' keeps running even while a kid is away at school or in the hospital.

ConceptTitle: Support Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: The support test for a qualifying child requires that the child did not provide more than half of their own support for the year. Unlike the qualifying relative test, it doesn't matter how much support the taxpayer themselves provided.
KeyPoints: Child must not have provided more than half of own support|Doesn't require the taxpayer to have provided the support|Scholarships are excluded when a full-time student is involved|Different from the qualifying relative support test

ConceptTitle: Support Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: This is the test people flip backwards. For a qualifying child, ask if the CHILD supported themselves - not whether the taxpayer paid for everything.

ConceptTitle: Support Test for a Qualifying Child
Content: Think of it this way: a qualifying child just can't be paying their own way through life. It doesn't matter if grandma paid half the bills - what matters is the kid didn't pay more than half.

A qualifying child generally cannot file a joint return with a spouse for the year, unless that joint return was filed only to claim a refund and no tax liability would exist for either spouse if filing separately.
KeyPoints: Filing jointly usually disqualifies a child as a dependent|Exception: joint return filed only to claim a refund|No tax liability for either spouse on separate returns|Rare exception, not the general rule

Content: The joint return test trips people up on the exception. A married teenager filing jointly ONLY to get a refund - with no real tax liability - can still be a qualifying child.
Think of the refund-only exception as a narrow loophole, not a general rule. If a married dependent files jointly just to collect withholding back, it usually doesn't break their dependent status.

ConceptTitle: Tie-Breaker Rules for a Qualifying Child
Content: When a child meets the tests for more than one taxpayer, tie-breaker rules decide who claims the child: a parent wins over a non-parent, and between two parents, the one the child lived with longer wins, or if equal, the parent with the higher AGI.
KeyPoints: A parent beats a non-parent claimant|Between two parents, longer residency wins|If residency is equal, higher AGI wins|Applies when more than one person could claim the same child

ConceptTitle: Tie-Breaker Rules for a Qualifying Child
Content: Tie-breaker questions always follow the same order: parent beats non-parent, longer residency wins between parents, and higher AGI breaks a residency tie.

ConceptTitle: Tie-Breaker Rules for a Qualifying Child
Content: Picture a simple flowchart: is a parent involved? Parent wins. Two parents? Whoever the kid lived with more wins. Dead even? Whoever earned more wins.

A qualifying child and a qualifying relative are two different paths to claiming a dependent. A qualifying child relies on relationship, age, and residency, while a qualifying relative relies on a broader relationship or household test plus a gross income limit.
KeyPoints: Two separate sets of tests for dependency|Qualifying child: age and residency driven|Qualifying relative: income limit driven|A person can only be claimed under one category, not both

Content: If a question gives you an age and a living arrangement, think qualifying child. If it gives you an income number, think qualifying relative.

Think of these as two different doors into the same room called 'dependent.' A young relative living with you walks through the qualifying child door; an older relative you support financially walks through the qualifying relative door.
A qualifying relative is a dependent who doesn't meet the qualifying child tests but meets a relationship or household test, a gross income test, and a support test.
KeyPoints: Used when someone doesn't qualify as a qualifying child|Relationship or household member test|Gross income test|Support test

Content: Qualifying relative has three tests to remember: relationship or household membership, gross income under the limit, and majority support from the taxpayer.

Think of qualifying relative as the backup category - when someone can't get in through the qualifying child door because of age or residency, this is the second door, with its own three-lock combination.

ConceptTitle: Gross Income Test for a Qualifying Relative
Content: A qualifying relative's gross income for the year must be below the annually adjusted exemption amount. If the person's income exceeds that limit, they cannot be claimed as a qualifying relative regardless of how much support the taxpayer provided.
KeyPoints: Gross income must be below the annual limit|Limit is set and adjusted each year|Exceeding the limit disqualifies them entirely|Applies regardless of support level

ConceptTitle: Gross Income Test for a Qualifying Relative
Content: No matter how much support was provided, going even one dollar over the gross income limit disqualifies a qualifying relative completely.

ConceptTitle: Gross Income Test for a Qualifying Relative
Content: Think of the gross income limit as a hard ceiling, not a guideline. Go over it by even a little, and the qualifying relative claim collapses no matter what else is true.

ConceptTitle: Support Test for a Qualifying Relative
Content: The taxpayer must provide more than half of the qualifying relative's total support for the year. This is the opposite emphasis from the qualifying child support test, which looks at whether the child supported themselves.
KeyPoints: Taxpayer must provide more than half of total support|Different focus than the qualifying child support test|Support includes housing, food, medical care, and more|Reverse of the qualifying child support logic

ConceptTitle: Support Test for a Qualifying Relative
Content: Flip the logic here from the qualifying child test: for a qualifying relative, it's about whether the TAXPAYER provided more than half of the support.

ConceptTitle: Support Test for a Qualifying Relative
Content: Think of it as a mirror image of the qualifying child support test - there, you ask if the dependent paid their own way; here, you ask if the taxpayer paid most of someone else's way.

ConceptTitle: Relationship or Household Test for a Qualifying Relative
Content: A qualifying relative must either be related to the taxpayer in a specific way (like a parent, sibling, or in-law) or have lived with the taxpayer as a member of the household for the entire year.
KeyPoints: Certain relatives qualify without living together|Unrelated people must live in the home all year|A temporary house guest generally doesn't qualify|Some relationships never qualify even living together

ConceptTitle: Relationship or Household Test for a Qualifying Relative
Content: This test has two doors in: certain relatives qualify no matter where they live, while anyone else must have lived in the home for the full year.

ConceptTitle: Relationship or Household Test for a Qualifying Relative
Content: Think of close relatives like parents and siblings as having a permanent pass - they don't need to live with you. Everyone else needs a full year's residency stamp on that pass.

When no single person provides more than half of someone's support, but a group together provides more than half, a Multiple Support Agreement lets one member who contributed more than 10% claim the dependent, as long as the others agree not to.
KeyPoints: Used when no one person provides over half of support|Group must together provide more than half|Claiming member must contribute more than 10%|Other qualifying contributors must sign Form 2120

Content: Multiple support questions always involve siblings splitting a parent's care. Remember the 10% threshold and Form 2120 to make it official.

Picture several siblings each chipping in for mom's expenses, with no one covering more than half alone. As long as one sibling contributed over 10% and the others sign off on Form 2120, that sibling can claim mom.

ConceptTitle: Not a Qualifying Child of Another Taxpayer
Content: A person cannot be claimed as a taxpayer's qualifying relative if that person is already a qualifying child of any other taxpayer for the year, even if that other taxpayer doesn't actually claim them.
KeyPoints: Being a potential qualifying child elsewhere blocks qualifying relative status|Applies even if the other taxpayer doesn't claim them|Prevents overlapping dependency claims|One of the required qualifying relative tests

ConceptTitle: Not a Qualifying Child of Another Taxpayer
Content: The exam tests this exact trap: even if nobody actually claims a child, being ELIGIBLE as someone else's qualifying child blocks a qualifying relative claim by anyone else.

ConceptTitle: Not a Qualifying Child of Another Taxpayer
Content: Think of it like a reserved parking spot - even if the reserved car never shows up, nobody else can park there. If a person could be someone's qualifying child, no one else can claim them as a qualifying relative.

When parents are divorced or separated, the custodial parent - the one the child lived with for more nights during the year - is generally entitled to claim the child, regardless of who provides more financial support.
KeyPoints: Custodial parent = more nights during the year|Support level doesn't determine custody for this purpose|Custodial parent can release the claim to the noncustodial parent|Applies specifically to divorced or legally separated parents

Content: For divorced parents, the exam wants nights, not dollars. Whoever the child slept at more often is the custodial parent, and that's who claims the child by default.
Think of it as a simple overnight count - not a spending tally. Count up the nights each parent had the child, and whoever wins that count is the default claimant.
Form 8332 lets a custodial parent formally release their claim to a child's dependency exemption and Child Tax Credit, allowing the noncustodial parent to claim the child instead.
KeyPoints: Signed by the custodial parent|Allows the noncustodial parent to claim the child|Can be for one year or multiple years|Attached to the noncustodial parent's return

Content: Form 8332 is the one document that flips the default rule - without it, the noncustodial parent can't claim the child even with a divorce decree that says otherwise.
Think of Form 8332 as a signed permission slip. The custodial parent hands it over, and only then can the noncustodial parent legally step in and claim the child.

ConceptTitle: Claiming a Dependent Who Files Their Own Return
Content: A taxpayer can still be claimed as someone else's dependent even if they file their own tax return, but on their own return they must indicate that someone else can claim them as a dependent.
KeyPoints: Being claimed doesn't prevent the dependent from filing|The dependent's own return must note they can be claimed|Affects the dependent's own standard deduction|Common for working students claimed by parents

ConceptTitle: Claiming a Dependent Who Files Their Own Return
Content: Being someone's dependent and filing your own return aren't mutually exclusive - the dependent just has to check the right box saying they can be claimed.

ConceptTitle: Claiming a Dependent Who Files Their Own Return
Content: Think of a college student with a part-time job - they can absolutely file their own return, but they still have to flag on it that mom and dad can claim them too.
The kiddie tax applies a parent's higher marginal tax rate to a child's unearned income above a certain threshold, preventing families from shifting investment income to a child's lower tax bracket.
KeyPoints: Applies to a child's unearned income above a threshold|Taxed at the parent's marginal rate instead of the child's|Designed to prevent income-shifting|Reported using Form 8615 in many cases

Content: The kiddie tax question always centers on unearned income - think interest, dividends, and capital gains - not wages from a summer job.
Think of the kiddie tax as closing a loophole: parents used to put investments in a kid's name to get a lower tax rate, so the law now taxes that unearned income at the parent's rate instead.

ConceptTitle: Consequences of a Dependent Claimed Incorrectly
Content: When two taxpayers claim the same dependent, the IRS will reject the second e-filed return and require paper filing, and ultimately only the taxpayer who meets the dependency tests is entitled to keep the claim.
KeyPoints: Duplicate claims trigger e-file rejection|Second filer must paper file|IRS resolves based on who actually meets the tests|Incorrect claims can be reversed and penalized

ConceptTitle: Consequences of a Dependent Claimed Incorrectly
Content: A duplicate dependent claim doesn't get worked out by whoever files first - the IRS eventually looks at who actually meets the tests, and the loser can face penalties.

ConceptTitle: Consequences of a Dependent Claimed Incorrectly
Content: Think of e-filing like a single ticket window - the first claim through gets processed, but the second gets bounced back to paper, and eventually the IRS sorts out who really qualifies.

Claiming a dependent correctly is often the gateway to major credits, including the Child Tax Credit, the Credit for Other Dependents, the Child and Dependent Care Credit, and Head of Household filing status.
KeyPoints: Child Tax Credit requires a qualifying child dependent|Credit for Other Dependents covers other dependents|Child and Dependent Care Credit requires a qualifying dependent|HOH status often depends on having a qualifying dependent

Content: Whenever a question mentions the Child Tax Credit, dependent care costs, or Head of Household, check the dependency rules first - they're the gateway to all of it.
Think of a qualifying dependent as a key that unlocks several doors at once: credits, filing status, and deductions can all hinge on getting this one determination right.

Every taxpayer and dependent listed on a return needs a valid Social Security Number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number. Some credits, like the Child Tax Credit, require a Social Security Number specifically.
KeyPoints: SSN or ITIN required for taxpayers and dependents|Some credits require an SSN specifically, not an ITIN|ITINs are issued to those ineligible for an SSN|Missing or mismatched numbers can delay a refund

Content: Watch for questions where a dependent only has an ITIN - that can block certain credits like the Child Tax Credit, which specifically requires a Social Security Number.
Think of an ITIN as a tax-only ID, not a full-access pass - it lets someone be listed on a return, but some credits still specifically require the real thing: a Social Security Number.

The name and Social Security Number on a return must match Social Security Administration records exactly, or the return can be rejected or processed with errors, especially after a legal name change.
KeyPoints: Name and SSN must match SSA records|Mismatches can cause rejection or delays|Common after marriage or divorce name changes|Update with the SSA before filing if a mismatch is likely

Content: Name-SSN mismatch questions almost always involve a recent marriage or divorce name change that wasn't updated with the SSA first.
Think of the SSA's records as the master list the IRS checks against - if your name on the return doesn't match that master list exactly, the system flags it before anything else gets processed.

A tax return must be signed by the taxpayer, and by both spouses if filing jointly, either with a physical signature on a paper return or an electronic signature via a PIN or prior-year AGI verification for e-filing.
KeyPoints: Both spouses must sign a joint return|Physical signature on paper returns|Electronic signature via PIN or prior-year AGI for e-file|An unsigned paper return is not considered filed

Content: Joint returns need both signatures, whether on paper or the electronic equivalent - one spouse signing alone doesn't make it a valid joint return.
Think of a joint return like a joint contract - both names need to be signed on, whether that's ink on paper or a PIN and prior-year AGI typed in for e-file.
E-filing is faster, has a lower error rate due to built-in math checks, and produces quicker refunds than paper filing, which the IRS processes manually and much more slowly.
KeyPoints: E-file is faster and has fewer math errors|Paper filing takes significantly longer to process|Most refunds from e-filed returns arrive within 21 days|Some situations still require paper filing

Content: E-file versus paper questions usually just want you to know e-file is faster, more accurate, and gets refunds out sooner.
Think of e-filing like a direct highway and paper filing like a long, winding backroad - both eventually arrive, but one is built for speed and the other just takes longer by nature.
A taxpayer who needs to correct a previously filed return uses Form 1040-X to file an amended return, which can be used to fix filing status, dependents, income, deductions, or credits.
KeyPoints: Form 1040-X is used to amend a return|Can correct filing status, dependents, income, deductions, or credits|Generally must be filed within a set time limit to claim a refund|Does not replace the original return - it corrects it

Content: If a scenario says a mistake was found after filing, the fix is Form 1040-X - not a brand new 1040.
Think of Form 1040-X as a correction slip attached to the original return, not a do-over. It tells the IRS exactly what changed and why, rather than starting from scratch.

Form W-2 reports an employee's taxable wages, tips, and other compensation for the year, with Box 1 showing the amount subject to federal income tax. Box 1 wages are usually lower than gross pay because pretax deductions like traditional 401(k) contributions and some health insurance premiums are excluded. Employers must furnish W-2s to employees by a set deadline early in the following year.
KeyPoints: W-2 reports wages tips and compensation|Box 1 shows wages subject to federal income tax|Pretax deductions reduce Box 1 below gross pay|Employers must issue W-2s early in the following year

Content: If a question asks which box shows federal taxable wages on a W-2 the answer is Box 1 - and remember it can be lower than gross pay due to pretax deductions.
Think of Box 1 as your paycheck after the tax-free stuff like pretax retirement contributions has already been carved out - it is the number the IRS actually taxes, not your full salary.

All tips an employee receives are taxable income, whether paid directly by customers, added to a credit card charge, or shared through a tip pool. Employees must report tips of a set monthly minimum or more from any single job to their employer, and the employer includes reported tips in Box 1 wages on the W-2. Unreported or allocated tips that were not reported to the employer must still be reported on the return using the appropriate form.
KeyPoints: All tips received are taxable income|Employees report tips to their employer monthly|Reported tips flow into W-2 Box 1 wages|Unreported tips must still be reported on the tax return

Content: If a scenario mentions tips that were never reported to the employer the taxpayer still owes tax on them and must report them separately on the return.
Think of tips like any other paycheck money - it does not matter if it came from a jar on the counter instead of a paycheck, the IRS still wants its share.

Bonuses, commissions, and other supplemental wages are fully taxable and are usually included in Box 1 of the W-2 along with regular wages. Employers may withhold federal income tax on supplemental wages using a flat percentage method instead of the regular withholding tables. The withholding method used does not change how the income is taxed on the return - it only affects how much was withheld during the year.
KeyPoints: Bonuses and commissions are fully taxable wages|Usually combined with regular wages in W-2 Box 1|Employers may use a flat withholding rate for supplemental wages|Withholding method does not change the actual tax owed

Content: A question testing bonus withholding is usually testing that the flat supplemental withholding rate affects withholding timing only, not the amount of tax ultimately owed.
Think of a bonus like a second helping of the same meal - it still counts as food eaten even though the employer might season the withholding on it a little differently.

Fringe benefits an employer provides, such as personal use of a company car or certain gift cards, are generally taxable and must be included in an employee's wages unless a specific exclusion applies. Common excludable fringe benefits include employer-provided health insurance and a limited amount of group-term life insurance coverage. When a fringe benefit is taxable, its fair market value is added to Box 1 wages on the W-2.
KeyPoints: Fringe benefits are taxable unless specifically excluded|Personal use of a company car is a common taxable example|Health insurance and limited group-term life coverage are commonly excluded|Taxable fringe benefit value gets added to W-2 Box 1

Content: When a question describes a benefit an employer gave an employee, check whether it falls under a specific exclusion - if not, assume it is taxable wages.
Think of fringe benefits like extra perks at a job - some are tax-free treats the law specifically allows, but anything not on that approved list gets added right back into taxable pay.

Sick pay received through an employer's insurance plan or a third-party insurer in place of wages during illness or disability is generally taxable to the extent the employer paid the premiums. If the employee paid the insurance premiums with after-tax dollars, the sick pay attributable to those premiums is not taxable. Third-party sick pay is often reported on a separate W-2 or in a distinct box, and the taxable and nontaxable portions must be tracked separately.
KeyPoints: Sick pay replacing wages is often taxable income|Taxability depends on who paid the insurance premiums|Employer-paid premiums make the benefit taxable|Employee-paid premiums with after-tax dollars make it nontaxable

Content: For sick pay questions the key fact to find is who paid the premiums - employer-paid premiums mean taxable sick pay, employee after-tax premiums mean it is not taxable.
Think of it like an insurance policy you paid for yourself versus one your employer paid for you - if you already paid tax on the money that bought the coverage, the payout should not be taxed again.

Nonqualified deferred compensation lets an employee postpone receiving part of their pay until a future year, but it is still tracked and can become taxable under specific timing rules even before it is actually paid out. Amounts that fail to meet the strict deferral rules can become immediately taxable, along with additional penalties. On the W-2, deferred compensation is tracked separately from regular wages so the timing of income recognition can be identified.
KeyPoints: Nonqualified deferred compensation delays receipt of pay|Strict timing rules govern when it becomes taxable|Failing the rules can trigger immediate tax plus penalties|Reported separately from regular W-2 wages

Content: If a question involves deferred compensation that violated its deferral election terms, expect the answer to involve immediate taxation and added penalties rather than the original planned payout year.

Think of nonqualified deferred compensation like a promise to pay yourself later - break the rules of that promise and the IRS can decide the money was really available to you all along, taxing it right now.

Schedule C is used to report income and expenses from a sole proprietorship or a business a taxpayer runs alone, including as a single-member LLC that has not elected corporate treatment. Gross receipts and returns and allowances are reported first, followed by the cost of goods sold and ordinary business expenses, resulting in net profit or loss. That net profit or loss then flows to the taxpayer's Form 1040 and is also used to calculate self-employment tax.
KeyPoints: Schedule C reports sole proprietorship business income|Also used by most single-member LLCs|Net profit or loss flows to Form 1040|Net profit is the starting point for self-employment tax

Content: Any question describing a taxpayer who runs their own unincorporated business points to Schedule C as the form used to report that income.
Think of Schedule C as the business's own mini tax return that lives inside the personal return, tallying up everything the business earned and spent before handing off the bottom line.

Form 1099-NEC reports nonemployee compensation paid to independent contractors and other self-employed individuals for services performed. A business must issue a 1099-NEC when it pays an individual a set minimum amount or more during the year for services. The income shown on a 1099-NEC is generally reported on Schedule C, not as wages.
KeyPoints: 1099-NEC reports nonemployee compensation|Issued by businesses paying independent contractors|Triggered once payments reach a set yearly minimum|Income is reported on Schedule C not as wages

Content: If a taxpayer receives a 1099-NEC, the income belongs on Schedule C as self-employment income, not on the wages line.
Think of a 1099-NEC as the self-employed version of a W-2 - it tells you what someone earned, but none of the usual payroll taxes have been withheld along the way.

Self-employment tax covers the Social Security and Medicare taxes that self-employed individuals would otherwise have split with an employer, and it applies once net earnings from self-employment reach a set minimum. It is calculated on net earnings from self-employment, which are generally net profit reduced by a small adjustment factor before applying the tax. Half of the self-employment tax is allowed as an adjustment to income on the taxpayer's return.
KeyPoints: Self-employment tax replaces the employer half of Social Security and Medicare|Applies once net self-employment earnings reach a set minimum|Calculated on an adjusted version of net profit|Half of the tax is deductible as an adjustment to income

Content: Remember that self-employment tax exists because a self-employed person has to cover both the employee and employer shares of Social Security and Medicare, and half of it is deductible above the line.

Think of self-employment tax as paying both sides of the payroll tax coin at once, since there is no employer around to split it with you - the deduction for half of it is the law's way of easing that double burden.

ConceptTitle: Deducting Ordinary and Necessary Business Expenses
Content: Business expenses are deductible on Schedule C only if they are ordinary and necessary for the trade or business - ordinary meaning common and accepted in that type of business, and necessary meaning helpful and appropriate for it. Personal expenses are not deductible even if they provide some incidental business benefit, and mixed-use expenses must be allocated between business and personal use. Good records supporting the business purpose and amount of each expense are essential if the deduction is ever questioned.
KeyPoints: Deductible expenses must be ordinary and necessary|Ordinary means common in that type of business|Necessary means helpful and appropriate for the business|Mixed-use expenses must be allocated between business and personal

ConceptTitle: Deducting Ordinary and Necessary Business Expenses
Content: When testing whether a Schedule C expense is deductible, apply the ordinary and necessary standard rather than whether the expense was merely helpful in a general sense.

ConceptTitle: Deducting Ordinary and Necessary Business Expenses
Content: Think of the ordinary and necessary test as asking two simple questions - would other people in this business normally spend money on this, and did it actually help run the business - if both are yes, it is likely deductible.

A home office deduction is available only for space used regularly and exclusively for business, such as a dedicated room used solely for work and not for personal purposes. Taxpayers can generally choose between a simplified method based on square footage and a regular method based on actual home expenses allocated by business-use percentage. Employees generally cannot claim a home office deduction, while self-employed taxpayers who meet the exclusive-use test can.
KeyPoints: Home office space must be used regularly and exclusively for business|A simplified method uses a square footage calculation|A regular method allocates actual home expenses|Self-employed taxpayers qualify but employees generally do not

Content: If a home office question mentions the space is also used for personal purposes like a guest bed, the exclusive-use test fails and no deduction is allowed.
Think of the exclusive-use rule like a locked door - once anything personal creeps into that room's use, the room stops qualifying as a true home office for tax purposes.

ConceptTitle: Quarterly Estimated Tax Payments for Self-Employed
Content: Because no employer withholds tax from self-employment income, self-employed taxpayers generally must make quarterly estimated tax payments to cover both income tax and self-employment tax throughout the year. Underpaying these estimated payments can result in an underpayment penalty, even if the full amount owed is paid with the return. Taxpayers can base estimated payments on their expected current-year tax or on a safe harbor tied to the prior year's tax liability.
KeyPoints: Self-employed taxpayers usually make quarterly estimated payments|Covers both income tax and self-employment tax|Underpayment can trigger a penalty even if paid in full by the deadline|Safe harbor based on prior-year tax can help avoid penalties

ConceptTitle: Quarterly Estimated Tax Payments for Self-Employed
Content: If a self-employed taxpayer only pays their full tax bill when filing and made no payments during the year, expect an underpayment penalty question.

ConceptTitle: Quarterly Estimated Tax Payments for Self-Employed
Content: Think of estimated payments as a self-employed person doing their own version of payroll withholding - pay along the way in chunks, or risk a penalty for waiting until the end.

Form 1099-INT reports interest income a taxpayer received during the year from sources such as banks, credit unions, and bonds. Most interest reported on a 1099-INT is taxable interest reported on the return as ordinary income. Payers must issue a 1099-INT once interest paid to a taxpayer reaches a set minimum amount for the year.
KeyPoints: 1099-INT reports interest income from banks and similar payers|Interest is generally taxable as ordinary income|Issued once interest paid reaches a set yearly minimum|Reported on the taxpayer's return as interest income

Content: A 1099-INT showing taxable interest is reported as ordinary income on the return, taxed at the taxpayer's regular tax rates.
Think of a 1099-INT as the bank telling the IRS exactly how much it paid you for letting your money sit there - and that payment is treated just like any other ordinary income.

Interest from most municipal bonds issued by state or local governments is exempt from federal income tax, even though it must still be reported on the return for informational purposes. Tax-exempt interest is not included in taxable income, but it can still affect other calculations, such as determining how much of a taxpayer's Social Security benefits are taxable. Some municipal bond interest may also be subject to alternative minimum tax depending on the type of bond.
KeyPoints: Municipal bond interest is generally exempt from federal tax|Still must be reported on the return for informational purposes|Not included in taxable income directly|Can affect other calculations like Social Security benefit taxability

Content: Tax-exempt interest is reported but not taxed - remember it still counts toward figuring how much Social Security income is taxable.

Think of tax-exempt interest like a guest who does not have to pay for dinner but still gets counted when the restaurant figures out how big the party is - it shows up on the return even though it escapes direct taxation.

Form 1099-DIV reports dividend income a taxpayer received from stocks, mutual funds, and similar investments during the year. Total ordinary dividends are reported in one box, while the portion that qualifies for preferential tax rates is broken out separately. All ordinary dividends are taxable and must be reported on the return even if they were automatically reinvested rather than paid out in cash.
KeyPoints: 1099-DIV reports dividend income from investments|Total ordinary dividends are shown in one box|A separate box breaks out qualified dividends|Reinvested dividends are still taxable

Content: Reinvested dividends are a classic trap - they are still fully taxable in the year received even though the taxpayer never touched the cash.

Think of a reinvested dividend like getting a paycheck and immediately using it to buy more company stock - you still earned the income first, so it is still taxable, even though the cash never sat in your pocket.

Qualified dividends are ordinary dividends that meet specific requirements, including being paid by a U.S. corporation or a qualifying foreign corporation and meeting a minimum holding period for the underlying stock. Qualified dividends are taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rates instead of ordinary income tax rates. On Form 1099-DIV, qualified dividends are reported in a separate box and are always a subset of total ordinary dividends.
KeyPoints: Qualified dividends meet specific holding period requirements|Must be paid by a US or qualifying foreign corporation|Taxed at long-term capital gains rates instead of ordinary rates|Always reported as a subset of total ordinary dividends

Content: If a dividend qualifies, it gets the more favorable capital gains tax rate instead of being taxed as ordinary income - the holding period is the detail most often tested.
Think of qualified dividends as ordinary dividends that earned a discount by being held long enough - meet the holding period rule and the tax rate drops to match long-term capital gains.

Schedule B is required when a taxpayer's total taxable interest or total ordinary dividends for the year each exceed a set threshold amount. It lists each payer and the amount received, providing a detailed breakdown that supports the totals reported on the return. Taxpayers with interest or dividends below the threshold can report the totals directly on the return without completing Schedule B.
KeyPoints: Schedule B is required above a set interest or dividend threshold|Lists each payer and amount separately|Applies separately to interest and to dividends|Below-threshold amounts can be reported without Schedule B

Content: If total interest or total dividends exceeds the threshold amount, Schedule B is required to itemize each payer.
Think of Schedule B as an itemized receipt the IRS wants once your interest or dividend income gets large enough to warrant seeing exactly where each dollar came from.

A capital gain or loss is short-term if the asset was held for one year or less before being sold, and long-term if it was held for more than one year. Short-term capital gains are taxed at ordinary income tax rates, while long-term capital gains generally receive preferential, lower tax rates. The holding period begins the day after the asset is acquired and includes the day it is sold.
KeyPoints: Assets held one year or less produce short-term gains or losses|Assets held more than one year produce long-term gains or losses|Short-term gains are taxed at ordinary rates|Long-term gains get preferential lower tax rates

Content: The one-year holding period is the dividing line - one year or less is short-term taxed as ordinary income, more than one year is long-term taxed at preferential rates.
Think of the holding period like a countdown - cross the one-year mark before selling and the gain switches from being taxed like a paycheck to getting a lower, more favorable tax rate.

Cost basis is generally the amount paid to acquire an asset, including the purchase price plus certain related costs such as commissions. Basis is used to calculate gain or loss when the asset is eventually sold, and it can be adjusted upward for improvements or downward for certain deductions taken over time. For inherited property, basis is typically adjusted to the fair market value at the date of death rather than what the original owner paid.
KeyPoints: Cost basis generally starts with the purchase price plus acquisition costs|Basis is used to calculate gain or loss on sale|Basis can be adjusted for improvements or prior deductions|Inherited property usually gets a stepped-up basis to fair market value

Content: Watch for inherited property questions - basis typically steps up to fair market value at death rather than carrying over the decedent's original cost.
Think of basis as the tax version of a receipt - it tracks what was really invested in an asset so that only the true profit above that amount gets taxed when it is sold.

Capital losses first offset capital gains, and any net capital loss beyond that can offset a limited amount of other income each year. A net capital loss that exceeds the annual limit against ordinary income is not lost - it carries forward to future tax years indefinitely until fully used. Short-term and long-term gains and losses are netted separately before being combined into an overall net capital gain or loss.
KeyPoints: Capital losses offset capital gains first|A limited amount of excess loss can offset other income each year|Unused losses carry forward to future years indefinitely|Short-term and long-term amounts are netted separately first

Content: If losses exceed the yearly limit against other income, the excess is not wasted - it carries forward to next year's return.
Think of a big capital loss like a gift card with no expiration date - if you cannot use it all this year, the remaining balance just rolls forward to use next year.

The wash sale rule disallows a loss deduction when a taxpayer sells a security at a loss and buys the same or a substantially identical security within a window of 30 days before or after the sale. The disallowed loss is not permanently lost - it is added to the basis of the newly purchased replacement security, deferring the loss until that new position is eventually sold. The rule applies across accounts, including purchases made in an IRA, and is intended to prevent taxpayers from claiming a loss while effectively maintaining the same investment position.
KeyPoints: Wash sale rule disallows losses on substantially identical securities|Applies within 30 days before or after the sale|Disallowed loss is added to the replacement security's basis|Rule can apply across different accounts including IRAs

Content: If a taxpayer sells a stock at a loss and repurchases the same or a substantially identical stock within the 61-day window around the sale, the loss is disallowed under the wash sale rule.

Think of the wash sale rule as the IRS saying you cannot claim you lost money on an investment if you basically kept the same bet running the whole time - the loss just gets tucked into the new shares instead of disappearing.

ConceptTitle: Form 1099-B and Covered vs Noncovered Basis
Content: Form 1099-B reports proceeds from broker transactions such as stock and security sales, and it typically indicates whether the security is covered or noncovered for basis reporting purposes. For covered securities, the broker is required to report the taxpayer's cost basis to both the taxpayer and the IRS. For noncovered securities, the broker may report proceeds but not basis, leaving the taxpayer responsible for determining and reporting the correct basis on their own.
KeyPoints: 1099-B reports proceeds from broker-handled security sales|Covered securities have broker-reported basis sent to the IRS|Noncovered securities may show proceeds only without reported basis|Taxpayer must determine basis themselves for noncovered securities

ConceptTitle: Form 1099-B and Covered vs Noncovered Basis
Content: If a 1099-B shows a noncovered security with no reported basis, the taxpayer is responsible for figuring out and reporting the correct basis themselves.

ConceptTitle: Form 1099-B and Covered vs Noncovered Basis
Content: Think of covered versus noncovered like a receipt that either came stapled to your purchase or got lost along the way - if it is covered the broker hands the IRS the receipt for you, if not, you have to dig up the proof yourself.

The net investment income tax is an additional tax that applies to certain investment income, such as interest, dividends, and capital gains, once a taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income exceeds a set threshold based on filing status. It applies on top of the regular income tax and capital gains tax already owed on that investment income. The tax generally applies to the smaller of net investment income or the amount by which modified adjusted gross income exceeds the applicable threshold.
KeyPoints: Net investment income tax is an additional tax on investment-type income|Applies once modified adjusted gross income exceeds a set threshold|Threshold varies by filing status|Tax applies to the smaller of net investment income or the excess over the threshold

Content: Net investment income tax questions test that this is an extra layer of tax above regular capital gains tax, triggered only once income crosses a filing-status-based threshold.

Think of the net investment income tax as a surcharge that kicks in for higher-income investors - it does not replace the regular tax on interest, dividends, and gains, it stacks an extra charge on top.

Social Security benefits may be partially taxable depending on a taxpayer's combined income, which includes adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest, and half of the Social Security benefits received. Depending on the combined income level and filing status, up to a certain maximum percentage of benefits can become taxable, but benefits are never fully taxable beyond that cap. Taxpayers with little other income often find that none of their Social Security benefits are taxable at all.
KeyPoints: Combined income determines how much of Social Security is taxable|Combined income includes AGI, tax-exempt interest, and half of benefits|A maximum percentage cap applies to how much can be taxed|Low-income taxpayers often owe no tax on their benefits

Content: Remember combined income - not just Social Security itself - drives taxability, and even at high income levels only a capped percentage of benefits can ever be taxed.

Think of combined income as a special mixing bowl that blends regular income with half of Social Security to test whether the benefits should be taxed - and even at the worst mix, only part of the benefit ever ends up taxable.

ConceptTitle: Combined Income and the Social Security Worksheet
Content: The Social Security benefits worksheet walks through the combined income calculation step by step, comparing combined income to two threshold levels that depend on filing status. Falling below the lower threshold means none of the benefits are taxable, falling between the two thresholds phases in a smaller taxable percentage, and exceeding the upper threshold can phase in the higher maximum taxable percentage. Filing as married filing separately while living with a spouse during the year generally eliminates the lower thresholds, often making benefits taxable at the higher rate regardless of income level.
KeyPoints: Worksheet compares combined income to two filing-status-based thresholds|Below the lower threshold means no benefits are taxable|Between the thresholds phases in a smaller taxable percentage|Married filing separately while living together often removes favorable thresholds

ConceptTitle: Combined Income and the Social Security Worksheet
Content: Watch for married filing separately taxpayers who lived with their spouse during the year - the worksheet often makes their Social Security benefits taxable regardless of how low their income is.

ConceptTitle: Combined Income and the Social Security Worksheet
Content: Think of the two thresholds like a two-step staircase - the lower step gets you to some benefits being taxed, the upper step raises how much more of it can be taxed, and choosing to file separately while living together can knock out the staircase's landings entirely.

Form 1099-R reports distributions a taxpayer received from pensions, annuities, retirement plans, and similar arrangements during the year. The form shows the gross distribution amount along with the taxable amount, which may be the same or may differ if part of the distribution represents a return of the taxpayer's own after-tax contributions. A distribution code on the form indicates the type of distribution, which affects how it is reported and whether any additional tax may apply.
KeyPoints: 1099-R reports distributions from pensions and retirement plans|Shows both gross distribution and taxable amount|Taxable amount may be less than gross if after-tax contributions were returned|A distribution code identifies the type of distribution

Content: On a 1099-R, always report the taxable amount shown, not automatically the gross distribution, since after-tax contributions can make the two figures differ.
Think of a 1099-R like a receipt that separates what you are getting back that you already paid tax on from what is genuinely new taxable income - only the new part gets taxed again.

ConceptTitle: Taxable Portion of Pension and Annuity Income
Content: When a taxpayer contributed after-tax dollars to a pension or annuity, part of each distribution represents a tax-free return of that investment, while the rest is taxable. A method for spreading the tax-free recovery of the investment evenly over the expected payments is used to determine how much of each distribution is nontaxable. If a taxpayer made no after-tax contributions, the entire pension or annuity distribution is generally fully taxable.
KeyPoints: After-tax contributions create a tax-free portion of pension distributions|A cost-recovery method spreads the tax-free amount over expected payments|Fully employer-funded pensions are generally entirely taxable|The taxable portion is reported as ordinary income

ConceptTitle: Taxable Portion of Pension and Annuity Income
Content: If the taxpayer never contributed after-tax dollars to a pension, treat the entire distribution as taxable - the tax-free recovery only applies when after-tax money went in.

ConceptTitle: Taxable Portion of Pension and Annuity Income
Content: Think of after-tax pension contributions like money you already paid a toll on once - each payment lets a small slice of that pre-paid toll come back to you tax-free before the rest counts as new income.

Rental real estate income and expenses are generally reported on Schedule E, which calculates net rental income or loss for each property. Common deductible rental expenses include mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and depreciation of the property. Rental income is generally not subject to self-employment tax, unlike income from an active trade or business.
KeyPoints: Rental income and expenses are reported on Schedule E|Deductible expenses include mortgage interest property taxes and insurance|Repairs and depreciation are also deductible rental expenses|Rental income is generally not subject to self-employment tax

Content: Rental real estate normally goes on Schedule E, and importantly, rental income by itself is not subject to self-employment tax.

Think of Schedule E as the landlord's version of Schedule C - it nets rental income against expenses like repairs and depreciation, just without the self-employment tax that a business schedule would carry.

Unemployment compensation received from a state or the federal government is taxable income and must be reported on the taxpayer's return. It is reported to the taxpayer on Form 1099-G, which shows the total amount of benefits paid during the year. Unemployment compensation is not subject to Social Security or Medicare tax, but it is included in taxable income for federal income tax purposes.
KeyPoints: Unemployment compensation is taxable federal income|Reported to the taxpayer on Form 1099-G|Not subject to Social Security or Medicare tax|Must be included as income on the tax return

Content: Unemployment benefits are taxable income reported via Form 1099-G, even though they are not subject to payroll-type taxes.
Think of unemployment benefits like a paycheck substitute from the government - it still counts as income the IRS wants to tax, even though no employer is involved.

Gambling winnings are fully taxable income and must be reported on the return, regardless of whether the payer issued a Form W-2G. Gambling losses can be deducted only as an itemized deduction and only up to the amount of gambling winnings reported for the year - losses can never create a net gambling loss deduction. Taxpayers must keep adequate records to substantiate both winnings and losses if they intend to claim a loss deduction.
KeyPoints: All gambling winnings are fully taxable income|A W-2G is not required for winnings to be taxable|Losses are deductible only as an itemized deduction|Loss deductions cannot exceed reported winnings

Content: Gambling losses can only offset gambling winnings as an itemized deduction and never create a net loss - winnings themselves are always fully taxable regardless of a W-2G.

Think of gambling losses like a refund limited to what you actually won - you can use losses to cancel out winnings on paper, but you can never turn a losing year into a deduction against your other income.

For divorce or separation agreements executed after 2018, alimony payments are not deductible by the payer and are not taxable income to the recipient, reversing the treatment that applied to older agreements. Agreements executed before 2019 generally keep their original tax treatment, where alimony is deductible by the payer and taxable to the recipient, unless the agreement is later modified to adopt the new rules. Child support, regardless of when the agreement was executed, has never been deductible or taxable.
KeyPoints: Post-2018 agreements make alimony nondeductible and nontaxable|Pre-2019 agreements generally keep the old deductible and taxable treatment|A modified pre-2019 agreement can adopt the new rules if it says so|Child support is never deductible or taxable regardless of date

Content: The key date is when the divorce or separation agreement was executed - after 2018 means alimony is not deductible or taxable, before 2019 generally keeps the old rule unless modified.

Think of the 2019 changeover like a line drawn in the sand - agreements signed after that line ignore alimony for tax purposes entirely, while older agreements keep playing by the old deduct-and-report rules unless they choose to switch.

When a lender forgives or cancels a debt a taxpayer owed, the canceled amount is generally treated as taxable income, reported to the taxpayer on Form 1099-C. Certain exceptions and exclusions can prevent cancellation of debt from being taxed, such as when the taxpayer was insolvent immediately before the cancellation or the debt was discharged in bankruptcy. Insolvency generally means the taxpayer's total liabilities exceeded the fair market value of their total assets immediately before the cancellation, and the exclusion is limited to the amount of that insolvency.
KeyPoints: Canceled debt is generally taxable income|Reported to the taxpayer on Form 1099-C|Insolvency immediately before cancellation can exclude some or all of the income|Bankruptcy discharge is another common exclusion

Content: If a taxpayer was insolvent immediately before a debt was canceled, some or all of the cancellation of debt income can be excluded up to the amount of that insolvency.

Think of canceled debt like a gift of money from the lender - the IRS usually treats forgiven debt as income, unless the taxpayer was already underwater on their finances or the debt vanished through bankruptcy, in which case the tax bill can be excused too.

Income from an activity carried on without a genuine profit motive is treated as hobby income rather than business income, and it must still be reported as taxable income even though it is not subject to self-employment tax. Unlike a business, expenses related to a hobby generally cannot be deducted to offset hobby income under current rules. Factors distinguishing a business from a hobby include whether the activity is run in a businesslike manner and whether the taxpayer depends on the income for their livelihood.
KeyPoints: Hobby income is taxable even without a profit motive|Not subject to self-employment tax like business income|Hobby expenses generally cannot be deducted against hobby income|Businesslike operation and reliance on income help distinguish a business from a hobby

Content: Hobby income must be reported in full as taxable income, but unlike Schedule C activities, hobby expenses generally cannot be deducted to reduce it.

Think of a hobby that happens to earn some money like a garage sale that keeps making a little cash - the IRS still wants that income reported, but it will not let you write off the cost of running your garage sale like a real business.

ConceptTitle: Jury Duty Pay and Other Miscellaneous Income
Content: Jury duty pay is taxable income and must be reported on the return, even though it is a small, occasional amount for most taxpayers. If an employer continues to pay an employee's regular salary during jury duty and requires the employee to turn over their jury duty pay to the employer, the employee may be able to deduct that surrendered amount as an adjustment to income. Other miscellaneous taxable income can include items such as found property or small awards that do not fit neatly into another income category.
KeyPoints: Jury duty pay is taxable income|Must be reported even if the amount is small|Pay surrendered to an employer may be deductible as an adjustment|Miscellaneous income covers amounts that do not fit other categories

ConceptTitle: Jury Duty Pay and Other Miscellaneous Income
Content: If an employee had to hand over jury duty pay to their employer because the employer kept paying their salary, that surrendered amount can be claimed as an adjustment to income.

ConceptTitle: Jury Duty Pay and Other Miscellaneous Income
Content: Think of jury duty pay like any small side income - it still counts as taxable, but if you had to give it straight to your employer in exchange for keeping your regular paycheck, the tax law lets you cancel that amount back out.

Prizes and awards, including cash and the fair market value of noncash prizes such as merchandise or trips, are generally taxable income to the recipient. This includes prizes won through contests, sweepstakes, raffles, and similar drawings, regardless of whether the recipient had to do anything to earn the prize. A payer may be required to issue a Form 1099-MISC if the value of a prize or award reaches a set minimum amount for the year.
KeyPoints: Prizes and awards are generally taxable income|Includes both cash and the fair market value of noncash prizes|Applies to contests sweepstakes and raffles|A 1099-MISC may be issued once value reaches a set minimum

Content: Winning a noncash prize like a car or trip still creates taxable income equal to its fair market value, not just cash prizes.

Think of winning a prize like getting handed cash equal to what the item is worth - even if you receive a trip or a television instead of a check, the tax law treats it the same as if you had won that much money outright.

A Traditional IRA is a personal retirement account that lets an individual set aside earned income for retirement, with contributions that may be tax-deductible and earnings that grow tax-deferred until withdrawal. Anyone with qualifying earned income can open one regardless of whether they also participate in an employer plan. Distributions in retirement are generally taxed as ordinary income.
KeyPoints: Personal retirement account funded with earned income|Contributions may be tax-deductible|Earnings grow tax-deferred until withdrawn|Distributions are taxed as ordinary income

Content: A Traditional IRA is funded with earned income, may allow a deduction, grows tax-deferred, and is taxed as ordinary income when distributed.
Think of a Traditional IRA as a savings account with a tax break built in now, where you settle up with the IRS later when the money comes out in retirement.

To contribute to a Traditional IRA, a taxpayer (or their spouse, for a spousal contribution) must have qualifying earned income at least equal to the amount contributed for the year. There is no upper age limit that blocks contributions, so a taxpayer can keep contributing as long as they have earned income. Investment income like interest, dividends, and rental income does not count as earned income for this purpose.
KeyPoints: Requires earned income at least equal to the contribution|No upper age limit prevents contributions|Spousal contributions use the working spouse's earned income|Investment income does not qualify as earned income

Content: Eligibility to contribute to an IRA is based on having earned income for the year, not on age or on having a workplace plan.
Think of earned income as the ticket needed to enter the IRA contribution game - without a paycheck (yours or your spouse's), you can't buy in.

Contributions to a Traditional IRA for a given tax year can be made up until the unextended filing deadline for that year's return, not December 31. This means a taxpayer can still fund a prior-year IRA contribution early in the following year, as long as it happens before the filing deadline and is properly designated for the earlier year. Filing an extension does not extend this contribution deadline.
KeyPoints: Deadline is the unextended filing deadline, not year-end|Prior-year contributions can be made early in the new year|Contribution must be designated for the correct tax year|Filing an extension does not extend the contribution deadline

Content: IRA contributions for a tax year can be made until the regular filing deadline of the following spring, even though the tax year already ended on December 31.
Think of the IRA contribution window as staying open a few months past New Year's Eve, closing only when the tax return itself is due.

ConceptTitle: Deductibility When Not Covered by a Workplace Plan
Content: A taxpayer who is not covered by an employer retirement plan can generally deduct their full Traditional IRA contribution regardless of income level. If the taxpayer is not covered but their spouse is covered by a workplace plan, the taxpayer's own deduction may still be limited based on their combined income. The deduction is taken as an adjustment to income, so it is available even to taxpayers who do not itemize.
KeyPoints: Not covered by a workplace plan generally allows a full deduction|Income level does not limit the deduction in this case|A covered spouse can still limit the other spouse's deduction|Deduction is an adjustment to income available without itemizing

ConceptTitle: Deductibility When Not Covered by a Workplace Plan
Content: If neither spouse is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the Traditional IRA deduction is not limited by income.

ConceptTitle: Deductibility When Not Covered by a Workplace Plan
Content: Think of it this way: if nobody in the household already has a work retirement plan, the IRA deduction door stays wide open no matter how much they earn.

ConceptTitle: Deductibility When Covered by a Workplace Plan
Content: When a taxpayer is an active participant in an employer retirement plan, their Traditional IRA deduction phases out over a range of modified adjusted gross income set by law, and can be eliminated entirely above that range. Active participation is generally shown by a marked retirement plan box on the taxpayer's Form W-2 for the year. Even when the deduction is reduced or lost, the taxpayer can still make a nondeductible contribution to the same IRA.
KeyPoints: Active plan participants face an income-based phase-out|Phase-out is measured by modified adjusted gross income|Active participation is often flagged on Form W-2|A lost deduction still allows a nondeductible contribution

ConceptTitle: Deductibility When Covered by a Workplace Plan
Content: Being an active participant in a workplace plan phases out the IRA deduction as income rises, but a nondeductible contribution is still allowed even if the deduction disappears.

ConceptTitle: Deductibility When Covered by a Workplace Plan
Content: Think of the workplace plan box on the W-2 as a flag that shrinks the IRA deduction as income climbs, rather than an outright ban on contributing.

A married taxpayer who is not an active participant in a workplace plan but whose spouse is a participant faces a separate, generally higher income phase-out range for deducting their own Traditional IRA contribution. This rule exists so that one spouse's access to a workplace plan does not automatically strip the other spouse of a deduction. Filing status matters here, since married filing separately generally faces a much narrower phase-out.
KeyPoints: Non-covered spouse of a covered spouse gets a separate phase-out range|That range is generally wider than the covered spouse's own range|Rule prevents one spouse's plan from fully blocking the other's deduction|Married filing separately usually has a much tighter phase-out

Content: When only one spouse is covered by a workplace plan, the uncovered spouse uses a different, more generous income phase-out for their own IRA deduction.
Think of the uncovered spouse as getting a separate lane with a longer runway, rather than being grounded just because their spouse already has a plan at work.

When a taxpayer makes a Traditional IRA contribution that is not deductible, either by choice or because income limits eliminated the deduction, the nondeductible amount must be reported on Form 8606 to establish basis in the account. This basis is tracked over the life of the account and is not taxed again when eventually distributed. Failing to file Form 8606 can result in that same money being taxed twice when it is later withdrawn.
KeyPoints: Nondeductible contributions are reported on Form 8606|Form 8606 establishes basis in the Traditional IRA|Basis is recovered tax-free when distributed|Skipping the form risks double taxation later

Content: A nondeductible Traditional IRA contribution must be reported on Form 8606 to preserve basis and avoid being taxed twice on the same money later.
Think of Form 8606 as a receipt proving the tax was already paid on that money, so the IRS does not try to collect on it a second time when it comes out.

A deductible Traditional IRA contribution is claimed as an adjustment to income, which lowers adjusted gross income directly rather than being taken as an itemized or standard deduction. Because it reduces AGI, it can also help a taxpayer qualify for other tax benefits that phase out based on AGI. The deduction is available whether or not the taxpayer itemizes deductions.
KeyPoints: Deductible IRA contributions are an adjustment to income|They reduce AGI, not just taxable income after AGI|Lower AGI can help other AGI-based benefits phase in|Available regardless of itemizing

Content: A deductible Traditional IRA contribution reduces AGI itself, which can be more valuable than a below-the-line deduction because it can unlock other AGI-based benefits.
Think of an AGI-reducing deduction as moving the finish line closer before other tax breaks even start measuring the distance.

A Roth IRA is a personal retirement account funded with after-tax dollars, meaning contributions are never deductible, but qualified distributions in retirement, including all earnings, come out completely tax-free. Contributions themselves can generally be withdrawn at any time without tax or penalty since they were already taxed. This makes the Roth IRA attractive to taxpayers who expect to be in the same or a higher tax bracket in retirement.
KeyPoints: Funded with after-tax dollars, never deductible|Qualified distributions are entirely tax-free|Contributions can generally be withdrawn anytime tax-free|Attractive for those expecting a similar or higher future bracket

Content: Roth IRA contributions are never deductible, but qualified distributions, including earnings, are completely tax-free.
Think of a Roth IRA as paying the tax bill upfront so the entire account, growth included, can come out tax-free later.

The ability to contribute directly to a Roth IRA phases out as modified adjusted gross income rises above thresholds set by law, and is eliminated entirely above the top of that range. Unlike the Traditional IRA deduction, this income limit applies whether or not the taxpayer is covered by a workplace plan. A taxpayer whose income is too high to contribute directly may still be able to convert Traditional IRA funds to a Roth IRA.
KeyPoints: Direct Roth contribution eligibility phases out by income|Applies regardless of workplace plan coverage|Eliminated entirely above the top of the range|High earners may still use a Roth conversion instead

Content: Roth IRA contribution eligibility is limited purely by income, unlike the Traditional IRA deduction, which also depends on workplace plan coverage.
Think of the Roth income limit as a separate gate that has nothing to do with a workplace plan - it only cares about how much you earn.
